title: Cool Flames and Low-Temperature Combustion in Microgravity Inform Advanced Engine Design
claim_in_our_words: The study of cool flames and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications.
verbatim_quote: Additionally, the study of ''cool flames'' and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications.
what_this_does_not_show: This does not show that cool flames occur in all materials, solid fabrics, or under high convective velocities, nor does it quantify cool flame ignition risks in spacecraft structural plastics.
implication_as_question: Could undetected low-temperature chemical oxidation persist in spacecraft ventilation ducts after standard optical fire detectors indicate complete flame extinguishment?

title: Absence of Buoyancy Yields Spherical Diffusion Reaction Zones
claim_in_our_words: In microgravity, the absence of natural buoyant convection prevents combustion exhaust from rising, causing flames in quiescent environments to form symmetric, spherical diffusion envelopes.
verbatim_quote: in microgravity, the burn rate is a little too slow, and we get that nice, you know, circular flame shape, and it’s very hard for the flame to sustain itself without the flow
source_name: NASA Johnson Space Center, Houston We Have a Podcast, Ep. 386
what_this_does_not_show: This does not show that microgravity flames are inherently benign; while quiescent spherical flames burn slowly in still air, gentle forced ventilation (such as 10-20 cm/s cabin circulation) supplies fresh oxygen and can sustain vigorous flame spread.
implication_as_question: How does the transition from buoyant upward plumes to spherical diffusion envelopes impact the spatial sensor placement and extinguishing agent dispersal inside spacecraft cabins?

title: Fabric Candidate Extinguishes in 1g but Sustains Burning in Lunar Gravity
claim_in_our_words: In parabolic flight testing of a fabric candidate under identical atmospheric conditions, the material ignited and self-extinguished in 1g, but ignited and sustained burning in lunar gravity.
verbatim_quote: And in 1g the flame ignites, but it self extinguishes pretty quickly. But in the lunar g test, it ignites and it keeps burning. And that was, I think, the first time we’ve seen that behavior in this particular material that it that it would extinguish in 1g but it would keep burning in lunar g.
source_name: NASA Johnson Space Center, Houston We Have a Podcast, Ep. 386
what_this_does_not_show: This does not prove that all materials burn faster or longer on the Moon, nor does it represent an official NASA design standard. A single parabolic-flight test on one fabric, described in a podcast; not PSI data; not generalizable.
implication_as_question: Could standard terrestrial (1g) flammability testing underestimate material fire spread risks inside pressurized lunar surface habitats?

title: Cool Diffusion Flames: Transition to Hot Flame and Oscillation in Microgravity
claim_in_our_words: Under microgravity aboard the ISS, gaseous cool diffusion flames exhibit complex extinction and transition kinetics: decreasing reactant flow causes extinction, while increasing flow causes a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.
verbatim_quote: Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.
what_this_does_not_show: This does not indicate that ambient cabin atmospheres support cool flames; it describes controlled gaseous burner injection kinetics aboard the ISS.
implication_as_question: Could fluctuating ventilation velocities inadvertently trigger a transition from low-temperature oxidation into a high-temperature hot flame inside spacecraft hardware?
